incidents.headline: Bandits kill 2 and abduct 18 in a Kaduna community

legal.context: Non-international armed conflict in the north-east (Boko Haram/ISWAP); banditry and communal violence elsewhere may fall under IHRL only
legal.why: Nigeria: Non-international armed conflict in the north-east (Boko Haram/ISWAP); banditry and communal violence elsewhere may fall under IHRL only. So IHL and war-crimes provisions apply only if an armed conflict exists; human rights law applies either way. Reported: alleged perpetrator Armed bandits; victims civilians, villagers; 2 killed. Civilians were reported killed. This engages the principle of distinction (ICRC Customary IHL Study, Rule 1) and the prohibition of murder (Rule 89; Common Article 3(1)(a) and Additional Protocol II, Arts 4 and 13). Rule 6 is listed because it is the test to apply if a party says the victims were taking a direct part in hostilities. Under human rights law it engages the right to life (ICCPR, Art. 6). People were reportedly abducted or held. Hostage-taking is prohibited (Rule 96; Common Article 3(1)(b); Additional Protocol II, Art. 4(2)(c)) and arbitrary deprivation of liberty is unlawful (Rule 99; ICCPR, Art. 9). The alleged perpetrator (Armed bandits) is a non-state actor: armed groups are bound by Common Article 3 and customary IHL, while human rights treaties bind the state, which must protect people and investigate. The Rome Statute provisions indicate which international crimes the facts could amount to; ICC jurisdiction depends on the state concerned.
